definition: Sanction severity increases with each repeated or more severe violation, up to removal.
Agents decide whether to help others based on the recipient's observed record with third parties.
Agents direct benefits to partners who previously cooperated with them and withhold them from those who did not.
Access to interactions, sales or privileges is reduced or removed when an agent's reputation falls below a threshold.
Agents choose which rule regime (e.g., with or without sanctions) they participate in, letting institutions compete for members.
Agents copy the behaviour of higher-payoff or expert others, so cooperative strategies spread by social learning.
A detected deviator (individual or subgroup) is expelled, blocked or quarantined from the group.
Agents or allocators choose interaction partners or task assignees using aggregated trust scores.
Agents carry identities certified or cryptographically verifiable so that reputation and accountability attach to a single persistent entity.
Access to a valued setting is granted only on proof of having performed the cooperative action.
Ratings or feedback about agents are aggregated into a running score visible to others.
A central planner agent learns and applies taxes, subsidies or extra rewards and punishments to align individual incentives with welfare.
The agents themselves propose and agree on the rules that govern them.
A shared resource allocation is decided by aggregating agents' votes.
Peers pay a cost to reduce the payoff of agents who defect or violate norms.
Agents post a stake that is partly or wholly destroyed if they are found to violate the rules.
Agents interact only with a fixed set of neighbours defined by a network.
After a failure, evidence is used to attribute responsibility to specific agents.
Agents are paid according to measured output or outcomes of their effort.
Agents can exchange non-binding messages before acting.
A shared, queryable record of agents' past behaviour is maintained and made available before interaction.
Agents publicly announce what they will do, making deviation visible and reputationally costly.
The set of actions an agent can take is limited in advance to prevent harmful behaviour.
A third-party adjudicator decides disputes or claims between agents.
Agents are equipped with internal machinery to create, spread, evaluate and comply with norms.
An agent publishes how others should treat messages that fail verification in its name.
Agents negotiate contracts whose conditional transfers are executed automatically.
An agent voluntarily makes backing out of a future cooperative action costly or impossible.
A safeguard filters out sanctions directed at cooperators (antisocial punishment).
A central algorithm assigns partners or resources from reported preferences instead of free negotiation.
A central monitor observes agents' behaviour and reports or acts on it.

code: central specification of roles and scope
definition: A coordinator assigns each agent explicit objectives, boundaries and resource limits.
The group jointly sanctions members who try to dominate or monopolize power.
When a step fails, compensating actions undo prior steps to restore consistency.
Joint rewards are distributed in proportion to each agent's measured contribution.
Agents incur costs or create future costs of backing down to make their commitments credible.
Deeper cooperation is sustained by a credible prospect of punishment for defection.
The cooperative option is made the default, requiring active choice to opt out.
Authority to make and enforce rules is devolved to smaller sub-communities.
Agents pay a deposit up front that is returned when they perform the cooperative action.
The population is made heterogeneous so that coordination on a collusive outcome is harder.
Group members elect a leader who guides collective decisions.
A fixed penalty is imposed on agents detected deviating.
Service is progressively degraded rather than cut when usage exceeds an allowance.
Interaction protocols are designed so that dishonest or uncooperative behaviour is not in agents' interest.
Agents infer which behaviours are disapproved by observing public sanctioning events and align their own sanctioning.
Resource users themselves regularly monitor rule compliance and sanction violators.
Tasks are assigned to other agents through market-based decisions informed by estimated competence.
Interactions among agents are observed and logged to detect misbehaviour.
A violator is required to restore the actual harm done rather than pay a generic fine.
Any agent can join a shared network and relay traffic for others.

code: option to opt out of game
definition: Agents may abstain from the joint activity and take a fixed outside payoff.
Agents are paid only if they are verified to have performed (or refrained from) the target behaviour.

code: payment released only on verified delivery
definition: Payment is finalized atomically only if the service is verified as delivered.
Agents share reports about third parties' behaviour to form reputations.
Reported misconduct is judged by a panel of peer reviewers who decide the sanction.
Agents' conduct is reviewed by their peers in a public forum, generating reputational pressure.
Agents affected by another's choice may reward or punish that agent after observing it.
Group members actively prevent or undo the selfish actions of other members.
Members pool resources that cover any member in need, without individual underwriting.
Parties fix in advance the penalty owed if an obligation is breached.
Each agent's individual actions are publicly revealed to the group.
An issuer publishes which credentials are revoked so relying parties stop trusting them.
All relevant actions are recorded in a public, tamper-evident log that anyone can audit.
The probability or severity of punishment is adjusted to the degree of detected defection.

code: refund plus bonus if threshold unmet
definition: Contributors are refunded with a bonus if a collective threshold is not reached, making contribution dominant.
Punished agents are allowed to counter-punish those who punished them.
A procedure corrects and reverses sanctions applied in error.
Reporters whose reports match the consensus are rewarded and dissenters are penalized.
The reward function is redesigned so that contributing effort is the equilibrium strategy.
Multiple independent evaluators' scores are combined with a rule robust to faulty evaluators.
Agents are assigned distinct identities or roles to induce complementary behaviour.
Members contribute regularly to a pool that is allocated to one member per round in rotation or by bidding.
Strategies compete and those with higher payoffs are selected and propagated.
A shared list of flagged agents is used by many parties to refuse their interactions automatically.
Agents receive visible status markers upon reaching specified levels of targeted activity.
Failures are recorded in a standardized report to diagnose causes and prevent recurrence.
Every detected violation reliably triggers an immediate, small sanction.
Institutional features such as membership, scope and centralization are chosen to fit the cooperation problem.
A peer can temporarily remove another agent from interaction.
Who may participate is temporarily narrowed to cool down conflict or abuse.
A neutral third party facilitates agreement between conflicting agents without imposing a ruling.
An unaffected observer pays to sanction agents who violate norms toward others.
Agents can observe interactions they are not part of, informing later partner choice.
Light audits screen agents and escalate suspicious cases to a stronger adjudicating committee.
Agents exchange services in credits valued by time, with every hour worth the same.
Rights are granted for a bounded period and lapse automatically unless renewed.
Each agent is assigned a secure, tradeable share of a capped total resource take.

code: voluntary transfer of reward to peers
definition: Agents may give part of their own reward to other agents.
A written statement of expected behaviour and enforcement provisions is adopted by a community.
